newsitem.title: COMOROS: Hijackers wanted to "make history", pilot says.
newsitem.headline: Hijackers wanted to "make history", pilot says.

text.p: The pilot of a hijacked Ethiopian Airlines plane that crashed off the Comoro Islands said on Sunday that the three men who tried to divert the craft to Australia wanted to "make history".
At least 59 people died when the Boeing 767, flight ET 961, crashed into the sea on Saturday after it ran out of fuel.
Fifty-two of the 175 passengers and crew survived, Marta Tilahun told Reuters from the airline's headquarters in Addis Ababa.
One hijacker was reported to have been armed with an axe. Another wielded a fire extinguisher. The third had what he said was a bomb in one hand and a whisky bottle in the other.
Among the survivors was the Ethiopian pilot, Leul Abate, 42, who suffered head injuries. He told Reuters from his bed at the El Maarouf hospital that there were three hijackers on board.
A U.S. official said the U.S. consul general in Bombay, Mr F. Huddle, and his wife also survived.
Top African television cameraman Mohamed Amin was believed to be among the passengers but his fate was still uncertain.
Amin, 53, of Reuters Television, won acclaim for bringing Ethiopia's disastrous 1984 famine to the eyes of the world.
The airline said it would issue a passenger list on Sunday.
Security sources on the island said Leul and the co-pilot had identified two of the hijackers among the survivors, and they were arrested. The fate of the third man was unknown.
Leul said one hijacker was wielding a small axe, apparently one kept in the plane for use in emergencies. A second carried a small fire extinguisher from the plane, wielding it as a weapon.
The third said he had a bomb in one hand, although Leul could not identify the object as such. In his other hand was a bottle of whisky.
They wanted to go to Australia but made no other demands, Leul said, adding: "The hijackers wanted to make history."
"They may be either Ethiopian, Djiboutian or Somalian -- they spoke French," Leul said.
He said the three forced their way into the cockpit and beat up the co-pilot, Yonas Mekuria, 35, before throwing him out into the main body of the aircraft.
At one point a hijacker tried to fly the plane himself and wrenched the headset from Leul.
As a result, the pilot said he was unable to speak to air control personnel as the plane neared the Comoros. Earlier reports said there was brief contact with the control tower, but it was then cut.
Witnesses on the Indian Ocean archipelago off Mozambique said a medical team and scuba divers from the nearby French Reunion Island were looking for more bodies and survivors.

Aviation sources in Nairobi said seven Britons, four French, three Italians, two Americans, eight Israelis and a Hungarian were among the passengers on the plane. The British foreign office said it believed eight Britons were aboard.

Diplomats in Addis Ababa identified the Hungarian as Hungary's ambassador to Ethiopia and Kenya while the Italian news agency ANSA said the Italian passengers included two employees at the Italian embassy in Addis Ababa.
The plane was hijacked on Saturday morning soon after it took off from Addis Ababa before its first scheduled stop in the Kenyan capital Nairobi en route to Abidjan via Brazzaville and Lagos.
Witnesses said the plane broke in two when it plunged into the sea. Airline officials said the fuselage was seen floating while the rear part had submerged.

"We saw the aircraft going down and down and down towards the hotel just in front of the main beach and then fall into the water...The aircraft is broken into two pieces," said Frederick Chretien, the manager of Hotel Le Galawa.
"The plane skimmed the ground, went over the Galawa hotel ...made a big noise and crashed," another witness said.
